source.title: Post-Grokking Collapse at the Representation-Readout Interface in Muon-Trained Transformers
source.authors: Ali Janati; K. El Maghraoui; Andrei Kanavalau; Anass Belfatmi

record.tranche_reason: Tests modular-arithmetic grokking with training and held-out accuracy in transformer settings, including a different optimizer configuration and training-set fractions.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported grokking timing and the Fourier-progress analysis. The paper's later post-grokking collapse experiments are not included as evidence about the initial delay: they measure a distinct later failure. Cited findings from other papers are not recorded.
record.test_reason: It trains transformers on modular addition (p=113, 30% split) and reports train memorization at steps 200–800 with sustained 95% test accuracy thousands of steps later. It compares training fractions and tracks a Fourier progress measure along an AdamW trajectory. Most of the paper is about post-grokking collapse, which bears on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but misplaced in emphasis. The authors conclude that Muon groks earlier in the tested configurations. Their main finding is that post-grokking collapse in unnormalized runs is caused by a damaging readout update driven by the feature mean, while task information stays linearly decodable. Correcting cross-entropy derivative errors prevents these failures through 100k steps. RMS-normalized runs fail through embeddings instead. Full-family Fourier filtering supplies answer-orbit structure, so perfect filtered accuracy does not identify a learned algorithm.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular-arithmetic transformer training and train/test accuracy, but studies Muon/AdamW routing and post-grokking collapse, with Fourier projections and additional numerical and representation-readout interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer and training fraction change reported grokking timing and outcome. Fourier-filtered accuracy depends on the task-aligned projection, which the authors show can provide answer-orbit structure even for a memorizer.

fits_no_version.finding: After grokking, Muon-trained (and some AdamW) runs repeatedly lose test and train accuracy. In unnormalized models this is localized to a readout update whose mean-dependent displacement reproduces the failure, and it is prevented by correcting float32 cross-entropy derivative errors. In RMS-normalized models it occurs through embedding updates even with accurate CE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-grokking generalization can collapse through numerical feature-mean inflation acting on adaptive readout updates, while linearly decodable task information survives.

fits_no_version.finding: At solved checkpoints, Muon spreads the representation across about 326 effective Fourier pairs against AdamW's about 5, with task-family power of 28% vs 91%. Matched branches from an identical state end up with different dominant frequencies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimizer changes the spectral dispersion of the learned modular-arithmetic representation, independently of whether the task is solved.

record.problems: The training-fraction comparison is limited to reported conditions and is not a systematic size sweep. Several timing results are single settings or aggregates over successful configurations, with no error bars stated. The Fourier-filtered accuracy is task-informed and the authors' memorizer control shows it does not alone identify an algorithm.
record.rows_left_out: Post-grokking collapse, numerical-correction, readout-swap, decoder, and architecture-control results were left out because they measure later failures or mechanisms rather than the initial grokking delay or gradual formation of the generalizing circuit. Numerous additional Fourier projections and spectral dispersion results were also left out; the paper cautions that these do not identify an algorithm.

untested.parts: No systematic training-set-size sweep; only 20% vs 30% at p=113. No full chance-to-perfect accuracy curves for most runs.
Removal of memorizing components (a cleanup phase) is not directly measured. The authors state that algorithm identification remains unresolved.
No non-algorithmic data, and no initialization-scale or lazy-to-rich manipulation.
No efficiency comparison, critical dataset size, or ungrokking test. The readout weight-decay sweep concerns collapse, not the delay.
Spectral dispersion differs between optimizers, but the authors explicitly decline to identify shared or different algorithms.

Numerical CE corrections are applied mainly after grokking to study collapse. Accurate-CE runs from initialization still grok, but memorization timing for those runs is not reported, so the delay is not shown.

missing.what: Intermediate AdamW-trajectory points: family share 1.66% / 11.08% and top-5-pair filtered accuracy 19.48% / 70.73% at steps 20k / 30k, while test accuracy is 0.29% / 2.08%
AdamW sweep: 4 of 11 configurations never grok; grok steps range from 6,300 to 62,900 across lr/wd
Width-64, p=113, 30% variant: AdamW 84,800 steps, Muon 17,700 steps to sustained 95%
Depth 2: Muon 2,300 vs AdamW 5,100 steps. Depth 4: Muon 52,600 steps; AdamW never sustains 95% within 300k steps
Accurate-CE runs from initialization still grok (subtraction confirmation at 10,500 steps; RMS accurate-CE at 10,000–19,900 steps); memorization step not reported

record.verdict_notes: Table 10's text extraction is scrambled; the first block (AdamW 31,000 / Muon 6,300) is the p=97 variant, confirmed by Table 13. This mislabels r6 and r8. The correct p=113, 30% comparators are Tables 8–9 (AdamW 8,200, Muon 5,400). Tranche T1, because task and train/test measures match the original; the optimizer differs. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test a systematic range of training-set sizes; the size comparison is limited to the reported 20% and 30% conditions. The paper reports grokking thresholds and timing rather than detailed chance-to-perfect accuracy curves for every run.

Does not establish that the measured Fourier component is a learned generalizing algorithm or directly measure removal of memorizing components. The authors show the filtering measure can also be perfect for lookup-table memorization.
No non-algorithmic datasets are tested, and the study does not test initialization-scale or lazy-to-rich controls.
No LLM pretraining or realistic-data fine-tuning is tested.
Does not test an efficiency account predicting a critical dataset size or ungrokking below it.
The study does not establish whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm; its Fourier and filtering analyses explicitly leave algorithm identification unresolved.
Numerical corrections are applied after grokking to study post-grokking failures, not to determine whether numerical or optimizer choices produce the initial grokking delay.

rows.subject: AdamW trajectory, depth-1 transformer
rows.operation_detail: Measured the addition-family share of non-constant Fourier power along training.
rows.measure: Task-aligned addition-family share of non-constant power.
rows.locator: Appendix L, Family power during grokking
rows.note: The paper reports this as preceding the test-accuracy jump.
rows.check: This is only the starting point of a trajectory. The text gives 1.05% → 1.66% (step 20k) → 11.08% (step 30k) → 70.62% (step 37k), while test accuracy is 0.30%, 0.29%, 2.08% and 100%. The rise to 11% while test is about 2% is the anticipating signal; those intermediate points are missing.

rows.subject: one-hot lookup-table memorizer
rows.operation_detail: Applied full addition-family Fourier filtering to a predictor storing training answers and outputting zero on unseen pairs.

conditions.value: full addition family with constant mode

rows.measure: Held-out accuracy before and after filtering.
rows.baseline: Raw held-out accuracy: 0.761–0.906% across the five splits.
rows.value: Filtered held-out accuracy: 100.000% in all five splits.
rows.note: This control shows perfect filtered accuracy can arise from memorization without a learned generalizing arithmetic algorithm.
rows.check: This is a constructed lookup-table control, not a trained network. It calibrates the filtered-accuracy measure rather than measuring V2's effect. It is kept linked to V2 only as the basis for the limits_scope verdict.

relationships.reason: Addition-family power share rises from 1.05% to 70.62%, already 11% while test is about 2%, before the jump to 100% (r9, r11). The authors call this compatible with the Nanda cleanup account.
relationships.display_finding: Addition-family power share rises from 1.05% to 70.62%, already reaching 11% while test accuracy is approximately 2%, before accuracy jumps to 100%.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: The longitudinal power-share increase precedes the test jump: 11.08% family power at step 30,000 with 2.08% test accuracy, then 70.62% and 100% at step 37,000. This supports the descriptive progress component; the authors characterize it as compatible with cleanup.

relationships.condition: Full-family Fourier-filtered accuracy as a progress measure
relationships.reason: Filtered accuracy is 95.14% while test is 0.30%, but a pure lookup memorizer also reaches 100% filtered accuracy (r10, r12). An early-high filtered measure therefore does not show that a generalizing circuit is forming.
relationships.display_finding: Filtered accuracy reached 95.14% while test accuracy was 0.30%, but a pure lookup memorizer reached 100% filtered accuracy, undermining its specificity for generalizing circuitry.
